To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the differential responses in cultured human lymphocytes of normal and cancer patients to bleomycin are the result of differential repair capability of the DNA damage caused by this mutagen.
differential mutagen susceptibility in human lymphocytes may be related to genetic susceptibility to neoplastic transformation.
the mutagen susceptibility in human lymphocytes is highly variable among individuals, and cancer patients have a higher incidence of individuals with high mutagen susceptibility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a simple, rapid, and reliable method for the assessment of mutagen susceptibility in humans.
the genetic basis of differential mutagen susceptibility and the possible relationship of this susceptibility to neoplastic transformation.
the study of mutagenesis and carcinogenesis, with particular emphasis on the genetic aspects of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of the cancer patients tested have a genetic deficiency in their DNA repair mechanism.
the majority of cancer patients are deficient in their ability to repair bleomycin-induced DNA damage in lymphocytes in culture.
the majority of normal individuals have a mean breaks per cells rate of about 0.40, and that the mean breaks per cell rates of cancer patients is significantly higher than that of normal individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer patients are more susceptible to bleomycin-induced chromosomal aberrations than are normal individuals.
cancer patients are more likely to be DNA repair deficient than normal individuals, and this deficiency could be one of the factors that predisposes them to neoplasia.
the incidence of cancer in the population is directly related to the incidence of DNA repair deficiencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there may be genetic differences between individuals with respect to DNA repair capability and that these differences may be associated with susceptibility to carcinogenesis.
the differential mutagen susceptibility in human populations may have important implications in cancer epidemiology and prevention.
cancer patients are at higher risk of developing secondary malignancy after exposure to mutagens, including radiation.
